comment_00_what: 🏛️ RECOMMENDED RoC CONFIG (Python) — generated by RuleOfCode {{ROC_VERSION}} for {{PROJECT_NAME}} on {{GENERATED_AT}}. This file is a REFERENCE, not the active config: RoC does not read it automatically. Use it with `npx ruleofcode audit --config ROC-RECOMMENDED.ruleofcode.config.json`, or carry its decisions over into your own ruleofcode.config.json. It is regenerated on every RoC upgrade.
comment_01_principle: PRINCIPLE: a silently disarmed gate is more dangerous than a missing gate. Three rules this config enforces: (1) NO includes whitelist — everything is scanned minus ignores, so that no new folder/package can stay invisible because someone forgot to add it. (2) notApplicable means 'this concern DOES NOT EXIST here' — NOT 'we haven't gotten to it yet'. Debt is shown as a warning, not hidden as a waiver. (3) Every waiver carries a reason; if it is temporary — it also carries a DATE and an OWNER.
comment_02_includes: ❌ NO includes.global — DELIBERATELY. A positive whitelist requires someone to remember to add every new package; when they forget, the code passes the audit because no one looked at it. Without a whitelist, a new package is covered from the day it is created.
comment_03_ignores: venv/cache/build artifacts only. Tests are NOT excluded globally — the Python laws check them deliberately (Strict Expected Failures, No Wall-Clock In Tests, Float Tolerance). If something needs to be hidden from a SPECIFIC law, use ignores.byRule with the law's slug (`roc laws --list`), not a global ignore.
comment_04_laws: THREE LEVELS, clearly separated: error = the line that is not crossed · warning = REAL DEBT, made VISIBLE (not waived) · notApplicable = the concern does not exist. failOnWarnings: true is the strongest safeguard — every warning fails the audit, INCLUDING laws that future versions of RoC add as warnings. If you are not yet at zero warnings, leave it false and burn down the debt via the ladder (comment_06).
comment_05_minLaws: minLawsChecked (law 226 Audit Liveness): the audit FAILS if it runs fewer laws than this threshold. Born from a real incident — RoC v7.5.1 ran ZERO laws and printed PASSED with exit 0. The value above is ~90% of those applicable to this stack today; raise it to your real post-waiver count once you know it (see `Total Laws Checked` in the output).
comment_06_ladder: 🪜 LADDER (warn→fix→error): run the audit once, record which laws light up as warnings and with how many violations. Burn them down one by one; once a law reaches 0, raise it to error in laws.severity — so it cannot come back. When ALL reach 0 → failOnWarnings: true and the gate is finally tightened. Do not hide a law in notApplicable to pass — that makes it invisible forever.
comment_07_new_laws: 🆕 Laws from v7.7.0 (the architecture batch), all warn-first — expect new warnings, that is the rollout: 228 Timezone-Aware Datetimes (naive datetime.now/utcnow/date.today) · 229 No Assert Guards (python -O strips the asserts — the guard must be a raise) · 230 Strict Expected Failures (xfail without strict=True passes silently FOREVER) · 231 No Wall-Clock In Domain · 233 No Silent Exception Swallowing (except: pass) · 234 bandit · 235 pip-audit · 236 Concurrency Boundaries · 237/238/239 (info: seeded randomness, wall-clock in tests, float ==).
comment_08_knobs: All allowlist knobs accept a glob or substring. They are left EMPTY deliberately — fill them in only when you have a real composition root/adapter, not to silence a law.
comment_09_golden: goldenPaths (law 232 Golden Fixture Immutability): declare your snapshot/golden files and any change to them will require an entry in GOLDEN-APPROVALS.md in the SAME change-set. A silent golden regeneration masks a regression — the code approves its own new behavior. Leave empty if you have no golden fixtures.
comment_10_cache: cache: false — a cached compliance result may report a stale PASSED. The audit is a gate, not a build step.
comment_04b_process_laws: ⚙️ PROCESS/ARTIFACT laws (lowered to warning in laws.severity): they look for ARTIFACTS — checklists, CI configs, incident docs, PR/commit conventions, MD footers — not properties of the code. That is why they are VISIBLE (warning) but do not block the gate. Decide for each: if the concern REALLY lives outside the repo (DevOps/org layer) → move it to notApplicable with a reason. If it does not live outside → burn it down and raise it to error. Do not leave them on warning forever — that is a waiting room, not a destination.
comment_04c_domain_laws: 🏗️ DOMAIN/INFRA laws (lowered to warning): they check concerns that may not exist at all in this project (SQL queries, APM, CDN, health endpoint, RBAC). Decide for each: there is NO such concern (e.g. you have no SQL DB) → notApplicable with a reason. It DOES exist → burn it down and raise it to error. Left on warning so they do not block the gate before you have decided — but stay visible.
comment_04d_stack_policy: 📄 DOCUMENTATION/TESTS (lowered to warning): real debt — visible, not hidden. Burn it down via the ladder.
comment_08b_exactEquality: 🎯 exactEqualityIn — DECLARE FILES, NOT DIRECTORIES. The rule (from the field): if the SOURCE code rounds at the boundary (round(pnl, 2) · round(pct, 4) · prices as multiples of a tick), exact comparison IS the contract and pytest.approx there would HIDE a one-cent regression → declare those test files by name. If the source does NOT round → use pytest.approx, not a declaration. Why per-file: a per-directory declaration (tests/**) kills the law for the whole suite and a new test file is born outside its scope. A per-file list means a new file falls UNDER the law by default — exactly what you want.
